hints: Notice that you are given p, V, T and mass, so think about which gas law lets you find moles and then $M_r$.
Use $pV = nRT$ with $R = 8.31$ to calculate $n = pV/RT$, watch the powers of 10 carefully.
Divide the sample mass by your moles to get $M_r$, then see how many 32.1 sulfur atoms fit into it.
walkthrough:
**Find moles from the ideal gas equation**

We treat sulfur vapour as an ideal gas here. Rearrange to find moles first.

$$pV = nRT \text{ so } n = \frac{pV}{RT}$$

**Put in the numbers carefully**

$p = 1.00 \times 10^{-4} \text{ Pa}$, $V = 2.08 \times 10^{6} \text{ m}^{3}$, $T = 2500 \text{ K}$ and $R = 8.31 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.

$$n = \frac{(1.00 \times 10^{-4}) \times (2.08 \times 10^{6})}{8.31 \times 2500} = \frac{208}{20775} \approx 0.0100 \text{ mol}$$

**Calculate $M_r$ and link to sulfur atoms**

Molar mass is mass divided by moles. One S atom has $A_r \approx 32.1$.

$$M_r = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.321}{0.0100} \approx 32.1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$$

**Deduce the molecular formula**

Since $32.1 / 32.1 = 1$, each molecule contains just one sulfur atom under these very hot, very low pressure conditions.

options.A: Correct. $M_r \approx 32.1$ matches the atomic mass of one S atom, so the formula is S. At very high temperature and very low pressure, larger $S_8$ rings break apart into single atoms.
options.B: Incorrect. $S_2$ would have $M_r \approx 64.2$. This would need about 0.005 mol in 0.321 g, double the moles actually found from $pV/RT$.
options.C: Incorrect. $S_4$ would have $M_r \approx 128.4$. Students choosing this may have made a power-of-ten slip in $pV$ or forgotten to divide by T.
options.D: Incorrect. $S_8$ with $M_r \approx 256.8$ is the familiar form of sulfur at room temperature, but not at 2500 K. High temperature favours dissociation into smaller molecules, and the calculation clearly gives a much smaller $M_r$.
